name: Single-Graft Distance Ladder
one_line: Keep the tuned incumbent training recipe as a conventional core, graft exactly one mechanism taken from a domain-stripped index at a controlled field distance, and let executed proxy results decide how far away the engine should reach.
mechanism: 1) Core. The current best tuned recipe R* (for OptiLex, the multi-epoch, regularized BabyLM baseline from FEASIBILITY.md) is split into about 8 facets: data selection/order, objective, architecture, optimizer, schedule, regularization, curriculum, precision. 2) Graft library. Build a one-time, cached index of mechanism skeletons in the style of Kulikowski (arXiv 2609.07595). Opus distils each paper into {problem structure, operation on abstract quantities, preconditions, typical effect}, with domain and method names removed. Papers are drawn from four distance bands defined by the OpenAlex field hierarchy, not by embeddings, to avoid circularity: B1 = LM-efficiency 2024-26; B2 = other ML (RL, vision, speech); B3 = adjacent computational fields (compression/information theory, numerical optimization, signal processing, caching/databases, compilers); B4 = distant sciences (statistical physics, neuroscience of replay/consolidation, ecology/population dynamics, control, auction/market design). 3) Graft operator. Thompson-sample a band. Sample a skeleton whose preconditions match one facet of R*. Opus writes an explicit structure-mapping table (which quantity in the training run plays each role in the skeleton, in the style of analogical reasoning) and then ONE minimal diff that touches ONE facet. Hard rejects: the diff touches more than one facet; or a facet-level retrieval against the B1 corpus finds the same mechanism already published. In the second case the idea is logged as 'collapsed-to-known' and relabelled B1, so distance cannot be faked. 4) Uzzi profile. For each graft, compute the co-occurrence z-scores of its component concepts (OpenAlex concepts, against a degree-preserving randomized null), then the median and 10th-percentile z. This tests whether 'high median conventionality plus one atypical tail' predicts executed success. 5) Execute each graft on the proxy with 3 paired seeds. Reward is the log data-efficiency multiplier vs R*, with FLOPs and NVML energy also logged. Update the band posterior. 6) Confirmed wins are merged into R*, so the core climbs a ladder and later grafts land on an ever more conventional, stronger core.
closest_prior_work: ERA (Aygun et al., arXiv 2509.06503): prompted pairwise recombination of two published methods in the same field; 24/55 recombinations beat both parents. Alien Space of Science (arXiv 2603.01092): anti-availability sampling of 3-atom combinations inside one ML vocabulary, execution judged by an LLM. Analogical Reasoning (Shen, Druckmann, Zou, arXiv 2605.11258): analogies generated by the LLM, not retrieved, with only a curated subset executed, all in biomedicine. Scideator (arXiv 2409.14634): facets retrieved at graded distances, evaluated by self-reported creativity support. Domain-stripped fingerprints (Kulikowski, arXiv 2609.07595): retrieval only. PaperGym (arXiv 2605.11532): targeted cross-domain seeds no better than random diverse seeds, judged by an LLM. DishCOVER (arXiv 2504.20643): structured recombination of recipes. The 3-arm knowledge-base A/B test already planned in OptiLex's IDEAS_FACTORY.md (no seeds / rare ML concepts / distant fields) is the closest in-house design; this proposal sharpens it.
why_novel: No published system treats field distance as a controlled, executed-outcome variable. That leaves open the conflict between Luo & Evans, who find the premium for filling gaps falls with order and favours small gaps in CS and formal/design fields, and Shi & Evans, who find distant 'expeditions' are 3.5x more likely to be hits. The operator is also asymmetric: a tuned conventional core plus exactly one atypical element, which is Uzzi's realized-impact profile. ERA and LLM 'combine X and Y' prompts instead blend two parents symmetrically, and Chen/Zhao/Cohan show LLMs already over-produce exactly that bridge/synthesis mode. Grafts come from a mechanism index stripped of domain vocabulary, not from topical embeddings, which Kulikowski shows retrieve 'the wrong signal'. The design has two built-in controls the literature lacks: a random-diverse-seed arm (the PaperGym null) and a collapse-to-known check after mapping. Finally, it is the first test of whether a bibliometric atypicality profile computed for machine-generated ideas predicts executed gains, a gap the map lists explicitly.
evidence_basis: Realized outcomes. Uzzi et al. 2013 (17.9M papers): high conventionality plus tail novelty gives 9.11 hits per 100, novelty without a conventional core 5.33 against a 5 background. METR's speedrun provenance analysis: imported ideas drove 6.7x of the 31x speedup, adapted 3.0x, invented 1.6x (single-analyst labels, order-dependent decomposition). ERA: 44% of recombinations beat both parents, and 29/55 recombinations beat every leaderboard entry against 1/12 co-scientist ideas (uncontrolled for difficulty). Karpathy nanochat Run 6 went from 1.80 h to 1.65 h only after the loop was pointed at an external source (modded-nanogpt). Shi & Evans 2023: expeditions 3.5x more likely to be hits in MEDLINE but not significant in patents, where boundary-crossing is routine. Wang/Veugelers/Stephan: the novelty payoff shows up in foreign fields (+62.37% odds), not the home field. Luo & Evans 2026: gap-filling premium weakest in formal/design fields; CS H0 slope -0.72 (abstract verified this session; slope from the map). Mechanism evidence. Chen/Zhao/Cohan 2026: LLM ideas are 47.1-64.2% 'Bridge Opportunity' vs 12.1% for humans, and synthesis/unification 22.5-38.7% vs 5.1% (taxonomy labels verified this session). Shen AR: a structured relational-mapping step lifts novel-solution rate from 21.6% ('look in other fields') to 50.4% (Claude Sonnet 4.5; LLM-judged, and judged reasonable 67% vs 86%). Kulikowski: average precision 0.222 for abstracts vs 0.557 for full fingerprints. Gideoni et al. and the Tao/AlphaEvolve study: domain knowledge in the prompt dominates the choice of search machinery. Cautions carried into the design: PaperGym's random-seed null; Kittur-lab analogies were 38% duds; Scideator users ignored far facets; SciMuse v4 found graph-selected concept pairs gave no gain over titles-only. That last result means the 'sample less-connected concepts' rationale in IDEAS_FACTORY.md needs updating and should be tested by execution, not assumed. Web search budget was exhausted in this session, so no new prior-art search beyond the map was possible.
first_experiment: Budget about $330-450. Phase 0 (no GPU, about $35). Build a 2,000-skeleton index, 500 per band, with batched Opus distillation. Run a realized-outcome backtest that needs no model: for each imported or adapted record in METR's 77-record speedrun CSV, assign the source field of the imported idea to a band. This gives the historical distance distribution of ideas that actually worked. Phase 1: six arms of 32 ideas each, fixed allocation (no bandit yet, for a clean comparison): B1, B2, B3, B4 grafts; R = random diverse seed (a random skeleton from any band, shown without the mapping or single-facet constraint: the PaperGym control); F = free synthesis ('propose one improvement to this recipe', the pilot's 'ask' condition). Claude Code headless implements each idea as a train.py diff. Run 3 paired seeds each: 576 runs at about $0.25. Candidate hits (point estimate at least 1.11x with one-sided p<0.1) are confirmed with 5 more seeds plus an independent second implementation, to guard against the implementation lottery. Pre-registered thresholds. (H1, graft machinery) Pooled graft arms must reach a confirmed hit rate at least 2x max(R, F), Fisher one-sided p<0.1. If not, the retrieval-and-mapping machinery is killed: PaperGym's null holds under execution, and diverse seeds are enough. (H2, distance shape) Pre-registered prediction from Luo & Evans and METR: hit rate in B1+B2 at least that of B3+B4. If B3+B4 reaches at least 1.5x the hit rate of B1+B2, distance favours expeditions in ML efficiency, and the default allocation moves to B3/B4. (Feasibility guard) If more than 40% of B4 grafts fail to implement, violate the one-facet rule, or collapse to known, B4 is marked infeasible at this core. (Inconclusive guard) If there are fewer than 8 confirmed hits across all 192 ideas, fall back to the continuous secondary outcome: mean log-multiplier per arm, with a Welch test across the 3-seed means. If that still shows no arm difference, rerun on a weaker core (the 1-epoch recipe) before drawing conclusions. The Uzzi quadrant analysis is exploratory and reported with its low power stated.
evaluation: Only executed outcomes decide. (1) Proxy tier-1 multipliers on data, FLOPs and measured energy, with paired seeds and an 8-seed confirmation. (2) Two independent implementations per hit. (3) Tier-2 replication at the full 10M words and one larger model size before anything counts as a finding; DataDecide suggests single-scale ranking gets about 80% of pairwise calls right, so about 1 in 5 promotions are expected to fail. (4) Novelty is measured as collision against a corpus frozen before the run, using facet-level reranking, with a human audit of the (few) hits only; no LLM novelty scores. (5) Realized-outcome backtest of the distance hypothesis on METR's speedrun provenance CSV. This measures history, not the model, so it is free of contamination. (6) The bandit's learned band posterior is reported against the matched-cost IID and sequential-sampling baselines that Gideoni et al. require.
cost_estimate: First experiment: about $330 expected, $450 ceiling. Index about $35. Generation and mapping about $15 (192 x ~$0.08). Implementation about $80 (192 x ~$0.4 with prompt caching). 576 proxy runs about $145. Confirmations about $60 (about 25 candidates x 8 runs, plus second implementations). Steady state: about $1.2-2.5 per executed graft (LLM plus 3-8 GPU runs), so 25 grafts per day is about $30-60 per day. Growing the index to about 15k papers costs about $250 once, plus daily refresh.
risks: (1) Hit rates against a strong, stacked incumbent may be near zero in every arm, so the band comparison is underpowered; hence the continuous secondary outcome and the weaker-core fallback. (2) Distant skeletons may be re-mapped by Opus onto a known ML method (e.g., 'replay' becomes 'multi-epoch'), faking distance; the post-mapping collapse check mitigates this but depends on retrieval recall (the MUSES and ResearchBench results show retrieval misses about half the true roots). (3) Kulikowski's fingerprint evidence is a small, single-author benchmark; skeleton quality is untested at this scale. (4) Proxy-scale wins may not transfer (Fantastic Optimizers: a 1.4x speedup shrank to 1.1x at 1.2B), and gains from far bands may be the most scale-fragile. (5) Uzzi, Shi & Evans and Luo & Evans are correlational citation studies; citations are not executed gains, and the conventional-core premium may reflect how easily readers absorb work rather than effectiveness. (6) The single-facet constraint may exclude valuable multi-facet mechanisms; logging them separately keeps that visible.

name: Residual-Seeded Abduction
one_line: Treat every executed run as a test of the model's own pre-registered forecast. Turn noise-gated forecast failures into explicit puzzles, have Opus propose competing mechanistic explanations that cheap discriminating probes adjudicate, and seed efficiency ideas only from explanations that survive.
mechanism: 1) Pre-registered forecasts. Before any run, Opus records a predicted data-efficiency multiplier with an 80% interval, plus a predicted diagnostic signature: which held-out loss buckets move (rare vs frequent tokens; per source, e.g. CHILDES vs BNC; early vs late training), and gradient-norm or loss-curve shape. Forecasts are blind to results and stored with the run. 2) Recalibration first. After the first batch, fit a monotone recalibration of the forecasts, because LLM effect forecasts are systematically optimistic (a 0.56x shrinkage in Hewitt/Ashokkumar; 68-83% false positives on nulls in Cui et al.). Otherwise every residual would be the same optimism bias. 3) Noise-gated surprise. z = (y - y_hat_cal) / sqrt(sigma_seed^2 + sigma_forecast^2), plus a sign flip and diagnostic-pattern mismatch. A candidate puzzle needs |z| > 2 AND reproduction with 3 extra seeds; the proxy's detection threshold is 1.11x at 3 seeds. The puzzle card also includes the nearest knowledge-base records, to confirm that the literature, not only Opus, predicted otherwise. 4) Abduction. Opus writes K = 4 mutually exclusive mechanistic explanations. One slot is reserved for 'harness artefact or bug', since the Station found a config that compiled code had silently ignored for months. Each explanation comes with a discriminating probe whose predicted outcome differs across explanations: an ablation, a dose-response, or a diagnostic measurement. Probes are 1-2 cheap runs each, scored by code-owned statistics, never by the analysis agent. This follows Robin, where the agent's own analysis reported 7.5-fold against a human re-analysis of 1.75-fold. Explanations get a Bayesian posterior from the probe outcomes. 5) Exploitation. An explanation with posterior above 0.6 is written to the knowledge base as a verified local law (law / scope / evidence, in the style of Theorizer). It then seeds a generator that must propose efficiency interventions which the law predicts will help and for which the literature retrieval finds no precedent. These go to the proxy lab. 6) The forecaster is re-conditioned on the accumulated laws, so new surprises move to the current edge of the engine's own ignorance. This is a curiosity loop that asks 'why' before it mutates.
closest_prior_work: Heuresis 'Curiosity' strategy (Antoniades et al., arXiv 2606.25198): the ideator predicts an outcome, surprise = |y - y_hat| / sigma_M, and anchors are sampled with weight exp(learning-progress/tau) x reward, then mutated directly. It was the only strategy that produced 'Minor Similarity' (NS=2) nanoGPT ideas, 20/200 vs zero for the other five, but it trailed Greedy on quality (verified from the HTML this session). AutoDiscovery (Agarwal et al., arXiv 2507.00310): Bayesian surprise (LLM belief shift after an experiment on an existing dataset) as the MCTS reward, with surprise as the product. HypoGeniC/HypoRefine: data plus literature hypothesis refinement for classification rules. ASI-Arch's Analyst agent; PACEvolve; Rehearse (outcome memory for the judge); Si et al. 2026 execution-guided evolution (performance-conditioned). Historical: KEKADA (Kulkarni & Simon 1988) modelled a surprise heuristic in Krebs's discovery (from memory, not verified from the primary source).
why_novel: In Heuresis Curiosity, surprise decides WHERE to mutate; the system never asks WHY the forecast failed, and quality suffered. In AutoDiscovery, surprise is the output being maximized. Here surprise is an input that triggers abduction. Competing explanations are adjudicated by executed, discriminating probes before any efficiency idea is generated, and success is measured by executed efficiency gains, not by belief shift. The generator is thereby aimed at the opportunity patterns LLMs under-produce ('Puzzle / Contradiction' and 'Explanation Gap' in the Chen/Zhao/Cohan taxonomy) instead of the bridge pattern they over-produce. It also has a structural novelty argument no prompt-based method has: explanations are conditioned on the engine's own unpublished run logs, and on the places where the literature-trained prior fails. They are therefore low-availability by construction, in the sense of Sourati & Evans, rather than relying on the model to be creative from its prior. Recalibrating before computing residuals, and reserving a 'bug' explanation class, are also absent from prior surprise-driven loops.
evidence_basis: Heuresis (2026, the closest in-domain test, verified this session): novel ideas never approached the best known-recipe scores, and every novel nanoGPT idea came from the surprise-driven strategy. AutoDiscovery: 0.67 of Bayesian-surprise-selected hypotheses were surprising to humans, vs 0.15 for prompted 'interestingness' and 0.11 for direct LLM surprisal. The annotators were Prolific STEM MS/PhD crowdworkers, and the pool was already LLM-surprising. ASI-Arch: the top SOTA gallery drew more components from the system's own experiment analysis (44.8% vs 37.7%) and fewer from 'originality' (6.6% vs 10.4%); provenance was LLM-classified. HypoRefine: literature plus data beat literature-only by 15.75% and data-only by 3.37%. Theorizer: literature-grounded novel predictions were later supported 61% vs 34% (LLM-judged support). SciPredict: frontier-model accuracy stays about 20% regardless of stated confidence, while experts go from about 5% to about 80% with their feasibility ratings. So the model's prior is uninformative about where it is wrong, and only executed residuals reveal it. METR: invented records rose to 33% after Jan 2025, once imports were exhausted. OptiLex's own proxy detects 1.11x at 3 seeds, so noise-gated surprise is measurable cheaply. Cautions carried into the design: Kosmos synthesis statements were only 57.9% accurate, and the Robin 7.5-fold vs 1.75-fold discrepancy; hence probes and code-owned statistics rather than trusting explanations. Web search budget was exhausted, so no prior-art search beyond the map and direct reads of Heuresis was possible.
first_experiment: Budget about $250 if run on top of the Single-Graft pool, about $370 standalone. Stage 1: 100 diverse ideas (reuse the executed pool from the first proposal if available), each with a blind Opus forecast (multiplier, interval, diagnostic signature), executed with 3 seeds (300 runs). Fit a recalibration on half the ideas and compute residuals on the other half, then swap. Stage 2: take the top 12 by |z| and rerun with 3 extra seeds; keep those still above |z| > 2 (target 8 puzzles). Stage 3: three arms at a matched budget of 150 GPU runs and the same LLM token cap. S (residual-seeded abduction): 8 puzzles x 4 explanations, about 64 probe runs, then about 28 efficiency ideas x 3 seeds. C (Heuresis-Curiosity replica): the same 8 surprising runs as parents, 'improve this' with no explanation or probe step, 50 ideas. P (performance-seeded, Si et al. style): the top 8 performers as parents, 50 ideas. Confirm hits as in the first proposal (8 seeds plus a second implementation). A hit is 'novel' when a facet-level retrieval against a frozen corpus finds no same-mechanism paper and a human audit of that hit agrees; only hits are audited. Pre-registered thresholds. Success: novel hits in S at least 2 AND at least (novel hits in P + 2), AND total hits in S at least 0.5x total hits in P. That is novelty without the quality collapse Heuresis reports. Mechanism check: at least 50% of the adjudicating probes confirm the explanation predicted to win, vs 25% chance for K = 4. Kill conditions: novel hits in S no greater than in C (abduction adds nothing beyond surprise-weighting); or fewer than 3 puzzles survive the noise gate (at proxy scale the recalibrated forecaster is not wrong in reproducible ways); or more than half of surviving puzzles resolve as harness bugs. In that last case the loop is kept only as a harness-audit tool, which is still a useful output.
evaluation: Execution only. (1) Confirmed proxy multipliers on data, FLOPs and NVML energy against the incumbent, with 8 seeds and 2 implementations. (2) Probe outcomes resolve explanations, graded by code-owned statistical tests on raw logs; the analysis agent never grades its own explanation. (3) Novelty by collision against a frozen, timestamped corpus plus a human audit of hits; no LLM novelty scores. (4) Tier-2 replication of any novel hit at 10M words and a larger model. (5) Forecaster calibration (Brier score and interval coverage) is tracked over time as a dividend. Surprises should migrate, and calibration on previously surprising regions should improve. If it does not, the laws are not real. (6) Optional external backtest: recompute surprises on public agent-run traces (the Prime Intellect speedrun runs are reported as public but this was not checked), testing whether large-residual runs precede the agents' later record-setting changes.
cost_estimate: First experiment: about $370 standalone. Stage 1 about $120: 100 ideas x about $0.46 LLM, plus 300 runs x $0.25. Noise gate about $10. Explanations and probe design about $5. Probe implementation and runs about $30. Three-arm efficiency ideas about $165: about 128 implementations x $0.4, plus 450 runs x $0.25. Confirmations about $40. About $250 if Stage 1 reuses the Single-Graft pool. Steady-state overhead on top of the lab: forecasts cost about $0.02 per run, and about 4-8 probe runs per puzzle. At 25 experiments per day, expect roughly 1-3 puzzles per day, about $5-15 per day extra.
risks: (1) Most residuals may be noise, forecaster bias or harness bugs rather than mechanism; the recalibration, the 3-seed noise gate and the reserved bug class mitigate this but may leave very few puzzles. (2) Opus may produce unfalsifiable or post-hoc explanations; requiring a discriminating probe with a pre-registered predicted outcome per explanation is the guard. (3) Surprise-seeded ideas may be novel but weak, reproducing the Heuresis optimization gap; pair with the Equal-Tuning proposal. (4) The counts are small (8 puzzles, tens of hits at most), so the first experiment can only detect a large effect. (5) Laws discovered at 7M parameters may be proxy artefacts (tokenizer or dataset quirks of BabyLM); tier-2 replication is mandatory before a law feeds generation at scale. (6) Explanations and generation come from the same model family, so shared blind spots can recur; a second-vendor explanation writer is a cheap extension.

name: Equal-Tuning Headroom Archive
one_line: Stop selecting ideas on first-shot results measured at the incumbent's co-adapted hyperparameters. Give each idea, and the incumbent, the same small successive-halving tuning ladder, select on the predicted tuned gap with a novelty-proportional tuning subsidy, and credit ideas through the realized results of their descendants.
mechanism: 1) First shot. Every idea runs once at the incumbent's hyperparameters (the current practice everywhere in the map). 2) Knobs. A cheap call names up to 2 idea-specific knobs (e.g. a mixing ratio, a threshold, a replay fraction). The ladder always includes the learning rate, plus one incumbent knob most likely to interact (weight decay or epochs). 3) Equal-tuning ladder. Successive halving at the idea level: 9 configurations at 1/3 budget, the top 3 at full budget with 2 seeds, the best confirmed with 3 more seeds. The incumbent is re-tuned with the same ladder, so every gap is tuned vs tuned. Tuning uses a selection split of the held-out data, and all reported numbers use a disjoint test split, which avoids the selection-on-noise failure Gideoni et al. document. 4) Headroom estimate. From the ladder, compute the expected-max tuning curve E[max over k trials] vs k (Dodge et al. 2019 style) for the idea and the incumbent. Estimate the asymptotic tuned gap and a bootstrap interval. The selection score is an upper confidence bound on that tuned gap, not the first-shot score. 5) Novelty subsidy. The ladder budget is scaled by the idea's distance from the incumbent's mechanism family (via the facet-retrieval collision score) times P(tuned gap > 0). The incumbent's hyperparameters were co-adapted to it, so first-shot comparisons are structurally biased against ideas that differ most. 6) Clade credit. The archive stores parent-child links, and parents are chosen by an estimate of Clade-Metaproductivity (HGM-style: descendants' tuned results, Thompson-sampled) rather than their own score. A novel stepping stone that is weak on its own but yields strong children keeps getting expanded. 7) Headroom predictor. Every completed ladder becomes a training example (features: first-shot result, first 1-2 rungs, idea family, diff size; target: tuned gap). Once the predictor ranks well, full ladders are run only where it is uncertain, returning the compute and energy spent.
closest_prior_work: Heuresis (arXiv 2606.25198) names this exact missing capability but proposes no mechanism (verified this session): search needs to tell 'whether it is weak because the mechanism itself is bad or because the first-attempt execution simply has not been optimized.' Huxley-Godel Machine (arXiv 2510.21614): Clade-Metaproductivity estimated for self-modifying coding agents only (abstract verified this session). Hyperband/ASHA successive halving (Li et al., JMLR 2018) allocates across hyperparameter configurations, not across research ideas. Dodge et al. 2019 'Show Your Work': expected validation performance vs tuning budget, used for reporting, not for selection inside a search loop (both from memory, not verified from primary). Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers (Wen et al.): equal tuning as an evaluation protocol for 10 optimizers, not a search loop. AdaEvolve local adaptation; DeepScientist UCB over LLM-surrogate scores; the Implementation Lottery audit (arXiv 2607.26587).
why_novel: Every idea-search system in the map (AlphaEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, CORAL, Heuresis, GEAR, DeepScientist, Si et al., autoresearch) selects on a single first-attempt result obtained at the incumbent's hyperparameters. The Prime Intellect run explicitly failed to re-tune baselines before testing new optimizers. This proposal makes equal-tuning expected-max curves the selection signal inside the search loop. It adds a tuning subsidy that grows with an idea's distance from the incumbent, to correct a co-adaptation bias against novelty that no system models. It applies clade (lineage) credit to research-idea lineages for the first time, since HGM covered coding-agent self-modification only. And it trains an idea-level headroom predictor on the engine's own ladders, directly targeting the quality-novelty frontier that Heuresis reports no search or Quality-Diversity strategy expanded.
evidence_basis: Heuresis: 3,222 scored runs, 0 'Original' ideas, only 1 novel idea in the top 10 by quality, and the authors attribute part of this to untuned first attempts (verified this session). HGM: an agent's own score predicts its descendants' productivity weakly (DGM r = 0.285 weighted on SWE-Verified-60), while the clade estimator reaches 0.778, with HGM beating DGM at lower CPU-hours (single runs, 60-task subset). Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers: claimed 1.4-2x optimizer speedups shrink to 1.1x at 1.2B once AdamW is tuned equally. Unequal tuning changes conclusions, and this proposal applies the same logic in the opposite direction, to under-tuned novel ideas. Prime Intellect: baselines not re-tuned before new optimizers were tested, and the human pruning/re-sweep alone added about 20 steps. Autoresearch creativity study: variable-level-novel edits were 37% of iterations but produced 62.8% of the improvement, while the rate of successful edits correlated negatively with final gain (r = -0.632, n = 6 models). Implementation Lottery: single-implementation winners reverse in 25.6-43.6% of decisions (idea ICC 0.51-0.61). TTT-Discover: removing archive reuse was far more damaging than removing RL (5274 vs 1203 us, n = 1 per arm), and best-of-25,600 was the worst arm, so reuse of stepping stones is the main lever. Si et al.: RL on mean execution reward collapsed to 2 ideas (119/128), which argues for max- and headroom-oriented selection. 'Evolution or Illusion': strategy rankings flip between 1 and 40 seeds. DataDecide: single small-scale ranking predicts about 80% of 1B pairwise winners, which bounds what tuned proxy results can promise.
first_experiment: Budget about $200-250: 'Does equal tuning reorder ideas?' Pool: the incumbent plus 30 already-implemented ideas (reuse from the first two proposals or the pilot). 10 are known recipes from the SWARM.md lever list; 20 are novel, meaning no facet-retrieval match. Each of the 31 gets the ladder: a 3x3 grid over learning rate and its main knob, 2 seeds at full budget, then the best configuration confirmed with 3 more seeds on the disjoint test split. That is about 21 runs per item, about 650 runs in total. Measure: (a) Spearman correlation between first-shot and tuned multipliers vs the re-tuned incumbent; (b) rescues: novel ideas below the incumbent at first shot that reach at least 1.11x over the re-tuned incumbent after tuning (confirmed at 5 seeds); (c) false wins: first-shot wins of 1.11x or more that vanish once the incumbent is re-tuned; (d) whether the rescue rate for novel ideas exceeds that for known recipes (the co-adaptation bias); (e) Spearman of the 3-trial expected-max extrapolation against the final tuned rank. Pre-registered thresholds. Proceed if (a) is below 0.7 AND at least one of: at least 3 of 20 novel ideas are rescued (15% or more), or at least 25% of first-shot wins are false. The headroom predictor is viable if (e) reaches 0.6 or more. Kill equal tuning as a selection mechanism if (a) is 0.85 or more AND there are zero rescues AND false wins are under 10%: single-shot selection is adequate at proxy scale, and the budget goes to generation instead. The clade-credit component is tested afterwards (about $400-800): two 40-generation lineage searches at a matched number of runs, with parent selection by own tuned score vs by estimated Clade-Metaproductivity. Pre-registered success: the CMP arm's best confirmed multiplier beats the other arm's, with the correlation between each node's own score and its descendants' best reported as in HGM Table 1.
evaluation: Execution only. (1) Tuned vs tuned multipliers on data, FLOPs and NVML energy, with a disjoint selection split and test split. (2) The ladder's own compute and energy are charged to each idea, so the engine is scored on the joint frontier per dollar and per kWh, not just best result. (3) Rescued ideas must replicate at tier 2 (10M words) and at 2 model sizes. Tuned hyperparameters are re-tuned at the larger scale, not transferred, because the Fantastic Optimizers result shows proxy-tuned gains can shrink with scale. (4) Seeds-by-iterations frontiers, and matched-cost IID and sequential-sampling baselines (Gideoni et al.), are reported for every search comparison. (5) Headroom-predictor accuracy is scored prospectively on ideas it has not seen, never on its training ladders. (6) Hacker-fixer audit of the ladder, since tuning is a new surface for reward hacking such as tuning on the test split or stopping at the first validation step.
cost_estimate: First experiment: about $165 for about 650 runs, about $15 for knob parametrization edits and knob-naming calls, about $20-40 for confirmations and re-implementations; about $200-250 total. The clade-credit follow-up is about $400-800. In steady state, the full ladder multiplies GPU cost per promoted idea by about 7-20x. Applied only to ideas that pass generation and dedupe (about 25 per day), that is about $40-120 per day of GPU before the headroom predictor starts trimming ladders. The subsidy is the lever that keeps it affordable: known-family ideas get a 3-configuration ladder and far-family ideas the full 9.
risks: (1) Cost and energy multiply, working against OptiLex's own frontier goal; if the predictor does not reach Spearman 0.6, the ladder stays expensive. (2) Tuning adds degrees of freedom, raising the risk of overfitting the proxy even with split data; a 3x3 grid on a 7M model may also be too coarse to find the real optimum for exotic ideas. (3) Hyperparameters tuned at the proxy scale may not transfer, so rescued ideas may be the most fragile promotions. (4) If novel ideas at proxy scale are genuinely weak (the Heuresis reading), the subsidy wastes compute; the kill thresholds catch this within about $250. (5) Clade credit needs many executed descendants; with expensive evaluations the estimate is noisy early, which is why it is tested second. (6) A learned headroom predictor used for selection invites Goodhart effects; its accuracy must be tracked prospectively and it must never be trained on the ideas it scores.

name: Planted-Mechanism Worlds (PMW): a procedurally generated discovery gym for training-efficiency ideas with known headroom
one_line: Generate synthetic LM-pretraining worlds that each hide one exploitable structure. The best intervention and its data-efficiency multiplier are known by construction and exist in no literature, so the engine's real invention ability (as opposed to recall) is scored by execution alone.
mechanism:
1) A world is a tuple (base data process P, planted structure S, oracle intervention I*, unique-token budget D, proxy config). P is a random PCFG, HMM mixture or program-trace language with a 2-4k vocabulary. S is composed at random from primitives, each with random parameters: a secret permutation-group action on token subsets that leaves P invariant; a latent mixture of one clean source and several corrupted copies of it; a hidden sub-token segmentation; a hidden deterministic channel; a compositional skill dependency. The generator computes I* from the secret: augment with the true group, reweight the true clean source, re-segment on the true boundaries, and so on.
2) Acceptance. The OptiLex proxy (the train.py architecture at about 3-7M parameters) measures M*, the effective-data multiplier of I* over the baseline, from held-out loss on P with 5 paired seeds. A world is kept only if 1.3x <= M* <= 3x, which is well above the calibrated 1.11x noise floor.
3) Distance label, defined by execution rather than by a judge. A fixed enumerative library L of about 40 generic interventions (dedup, loss- or perplexity-reweighting, random-token augmentation, length or loss curricula, epoch and weight-decay sweeps, cluster-ID conditioning, and so on) runs with the same run budget the agents get. The world is NEAR if best-of-L recovers >=50% of log M*, and ALIEN if best-of-L recovers <=20% while I* recovers 100%. NULL worlds have no S, so M* = 1 by construction.
4) Sandbox. The agent sees train.py and the sampled corpus, and nothing else: generator code and secrets live on a separate machine. It may compute any statistic on the corpus and run up to B = 20 proxy runs. It submits a patch plus a structured claim in a small DSL, for example a claimed orbit partition or claimed source weights.
5) Frozen evaluator. It uses 5 fresh seeds and a hidden held-out sample from P. The multiplier is read off the world's loss-vs-data curve, which was fitted at 3 budgets during construction. Promotion uses an anytime-valid e-value test, in the style of the frozen referee in arXiv 2609.27051, so repeated submissions cannot p-hack.
6) Scores, none of them from an LLM. Headroom recovered HR = log M_achieved / log M*. Structure identification = adjusted Rand index (or exact match) between the DSL claim and the secret. False-discovery rate on null worlds. Runs and NVML joules needed to reach HR >= 0.5.
7) New world seeds are drawn each evaluation round, so the benchmark cannot be memorized or overfit.
closest_prior_work: DiscoveryWorld (arXiv 2406.06769): 120 parametric text-simulation tasks with implicit ground truth. BoxingGym (arXiv 2501.01540): 10 fixed generative-model environments for experimental design. HypoBench and LLM-SRBench LSR-Synth: planted hypotheses and equations; an audit (arXiv 2607.28684) shows a fixed operator library solves most LSR-Synth tasks. 'Propose, Don't Judge' (arXiv 2609.27051, 22 Sep 2026): synthetic finance worlds with planted true factors and an anytime-valid frozen referee. 'Discovery under Hypothesis Redundancy' (arXiv 2606.14386): signal-planting experiments. NanoGPT-Bench (github.com/IntologyAI/NanoGPT-Bench): real, time-split, but contaminable once records are public.
why_novel: Existing planted-truth benchmarks plant the answer in a simulated world, a dataset or an equation. None plants it in the data-generating process of an actual neural-network training run, where the thing to discover is a training-efficiency intervention and the headroom multiplier is known and measured per world. PMW adds four things none of them has together. (a) A literature-distance knob defined operationally: 'alien' means a fixed library of generic interventions cannot recover the headroom. That separates recall (near worlds) from invention (alien worlds), which no real-literature backtest can do, and needs no LLM-judged novelty. (b) Null worlds, which measure the false-discovery rate. (c) A mandatory enumerative-library control, which answers the 'Dictionaries, Not Darwin' and LSR-Synth critique. (d) Infinite procedural refresh, so the benchmark is contamination-free by construction despite Opus 5.5's roughly June-2026 cutoff. Prior art was checked via arXiv API queries only (web search budget exhausted), so 'not found' does not mean 'confirmed absent'.
evidence_basis:
The binding weakness is invention, not execution:
- Heuresis: 0 of 3,222 executed runs were rated Original.
- Prime Intellect: the novelty-gated run 'cannot improve the baseline', and 'None of the runs produced a fundamentally new method'.
- NanoGPT-Bench: agents recovered 9.3% of human progress, versus about 77% algorithmic human records.
- Opus 5.5 card: 'mostly tests incremental ideas'.

A benchmark that isolates invention is therefore the measurement OptiLex needs. Real time-split backtests are starved for Opus 5.5 (about 3 months of clean literature), and date-filtered search leaked the answer for 41% (Google) and 55% (DuckDuckGo) of questions. Synthetic worlds avoid both problems.

The enumerative control is essential: a fixed vocabulary solves most LSR-Synth tasks, and set-level selection solved 165-169 of 717 cells versus 74-78 for LLM evolution.

Noise-aware, many-item evaluation is needed:
- Evolution or Illusion: rankings flip between 1 and 40 seeds.
- Gideoni et al.: selection on evaluation noise, with a recommendation of >=300 items and 95% CIs.

Cheap procedural worlds supply that volume.

The structure-claim check targets the weakest layer: Kosmos synthesis/interpretation statements were only 57.9% accurate.

Our proxy detects 1.11x with 3 seeds and recovered a known 3.4x effect (p=3e-4), so the 1.3-3x worlds are measurable.

Verified this session from arXiv abstracts: 2406.06769, 2501.01540, 2609.27051, 2606.14386. Other numbers come from the adversarially checked map. verified_from_primary = false for the $0.25/test proxy cost (an unmeasured estimate).
cost_estimate: First experiment ≈$290-420 (GPU at an estimated ≈$0.013-0.08 per tiny-model run, plus ≈$220 of Opus 5.5 tokens with prompt caching). Full library of about 60 validated worlds: ≈$1.5-2.5k one-off. After that, ≈$250-400 per harness evaluation on 16-20 fresh worlds, so about 5 harness variants can be compared for about $2k.
risks:
1) Synthetic-to-real validity. Planted structures may reward data-analysis tricks that never occur in natural text. Mitigation: the validity-bridge gate; do not optimize the engine against PMW until it passes.
2) Leakage of the secret through sandbox mistakes, or structures that are statistically obvious. Mitigation: separate-machine generation, and red-team audits of whether library or statistics-only probes solve worlds.
3) 'Alien' worlds may be solvable only by exotic interventions that are useless in reality, or may be impossible to build with headroom above 1.3x.
4) Once the family grammar becomes known, the engine may overfit to the primitive set. Mitigation: hold out primitive families for test rounds.
5) Small n per round (6 alien worlds) gives low power, so worlds must accumulate across rounds.
6) Prior-art check was limited to arXiv API searches.

name: Contemporaneous Human-Stream Parity (CHSP): the post-cutoff human research stream as an executed control arm
one_line: Each week, turn newly posted post-cutoff arXiv efficiency ideas into results-stripped cards, execute them blind alongside engine and bare-Opus ideas under identical 3-implementation, equal-tuning protocols on the proxy, and score the generator as a probability of beating what the field is publishing now. All critic predictions are frozen and hashed before execution.
closest_prior_work: Si et al., 'The Ideation-Execution Gap' (arXiv 2506.20803): human experts spent about 100 h per idea executing commissioned LLM-written vs expert-written NLP-prompting ideas, and rankings flipped. PaperBench (arXiv 2504.01848): replicating ICML 2024 papers, graded by LLM rubric (21.0% best). NanoGPT-Bench: later human records as ground truth, scored as progress recovered. Wen et al. (arXiv 2506.00794) and Mule et al. (arXiv 2605.21491): labels taken from published benchmark numbers. HindSight (arXiv 2603.15164): time-split embedding match to future papers. Bolton & Torr (arXiv 2608.03569, 4 Aug 2026): fast-moving domains (F1 2026 designs, Magic: The Gathering Pro Tour decks) as contamination-free match targets. The implementation lottery (arXiv 2607.26587): 3 implementations per idea. COS Predicting Replicability Challenge: prospective predictions on unreleased replications.
evidence_basis:
Only execution resolves idea quality:
- Rankings flip after execution (Ideation-Execution Gap).
- Prompted o3 is at chance at predicting empirical winners, while fine-tuned predictors reach 64-77% (Wen, Mule).
- LLM-judged innovativeness correlates -0.06 with effectiveness (MLRC-Bench).
- Our Opus judge agreed with itself on novelty only 53% of the time.

One implementation is not one idea: implementation explains 33-45% of variance versus 4-6% for reruns, winners reverse in 25.6-43.6% of decisions, and idea ICC is 0.51-0.61 (verified this session: arXiv 2607.26587).

Optimization gap: novel ideas are compared against tuned known recipes (Heuresis), and optimizer gains shrink from 1.4x to 1.1x under fair tuning.

Revalidation is essential: 40-50% of agent gains vanish on review (METR), and the top Prime Intellect runs were the ones that measured noise.

Contamination: the Opus 5.5 cutoff is about June 2026, and date-filtered search revealed answers for 41% and 55% of questions, hence the frozen snapshot.

Time-split matching gives false zeros and correlates rho = -0.29 with judged novelty (HindSight, verified 2603.15164). Small-scale runs pick the 1B winner about 80% of the time (DataDecide), so the proxy is a meaningful though imperfect referee.

DeepScientist never reported whether pre-execution scores predicted outcomes. The frozen ledger closes that gap.

verified_from_primary = false for the Opus 5.5 cutoff date (taken from model info) and the proxy cost (an estimate).
first_experiment:
Arms (15 cards each):
- 15 randomly sampled human cards from arXiv first versions dated 2026-07-01 to 2026-09-24 that pass the eligibility filter;
- 15 engine-v0 cards (the pilot's noisy and ask generators plus dedupe);
- 15 bare Opus 5.5 cards, with generation tokens matched to engine-v0.

Plus 30 human placebo/test cards for the recall-discontinuity check (matching only, not executed).

Freeze and hash the critic predictions: Opus rubric ×2 passes and a pairwise BT tournament.

Execute 45 cards × 3 implementations × 2 tuning configs × 3 paired seeds = 810 proxy runs (≈$65-200 GPU) and 135 implementations (≈$170 at about $1.25 each). Card distillation, canonicalization and critics ≈$25. Total ≈$260-400.

Pre-stated thresholds:
H1 (idea value is measurable): idea-level ICC >= 0.5 with lower 90% bound > 0.3. If ICC < 0.3, single-implementation labels are declared invalid for efficiency ideas; that is itself a publishable finding, and CHSP then moves to 5 implementations.
H2 (the yardstick works): >=25% of human-stream cards beat the tuned baseline by >=1.11x at proxy scale. If <10%, the eligibility filter fails and is redesigned.
H3 (falsifiable prediction from the literature): the prompted Opus rubric's prospective AUC for 'beats 1.11x' is <=0.60. If it is >=0.70, the chance-level finding does not hold for Opus 5.5 in this domain, and the cheap judge becomes admissible as a filter.

Report P(engine > human) and P(bare > human) with bootstrap CIs. At n=15 these are instrument calibration, not a verdict.
evaluation:
Referees are execution-measured effective-data multipliers on hidden held-out loss (plus measured FLOPs and joules) from a frozen, code-owned evaluator. Every AI idea is compared against real human research published after the model's cutoff, executed identically.

Critic validity is assessed only prospectively, against these executed outcomes, via predictions that were hashed and committed before execution.

No LLM judge decides any outcome. LLMs only implement, canonicalize and are the subjects under test.
cost_estimate: Pilot ≈$260-400. Steady state ≈$6-9 per executed idea: 3 implementations at about $1.25 each, plus 18 runs at an estimated $0.08-0.25, plus about $0.3 for card and critic calls. That is ≈$200-280 per week for 30 ideas (10 per arm), and ≈$2.5-3.5k over 3 months, producing about 360 multi-implementation, contamination-free outcome labels, about 8x Wen et al.'s expert-comparison set.
risks:
1) Selection bias. Only human ideas that fit proxy scale are eligible, so the human arm under-represents scale-dependent ideas, and survivorship makes it a stricter bar than raw human ideation.
2) Card distillation can inject the distiller's priors or lose key details. Mitigation: human fidelity checks, and an optional check with the authors on a few cards.
3) Proxy-to-scale transfer is imperfect (about 20% of pairwise calls wrong in DataDecide), so parity at 7-20M parameters may not hold at scale. Promote the top decile to tier 2.
4) Implementers based on Opus may implement ideas resembling their own priors better (a source bias despite blinding). Monitor per-arm implementation-failure rates.
5) Small weekly n and a moving human distribution. Accumulate, and report per-quarter parity.
6) A leaky frozen snapshot would contaminate the AI arms. Audit with the recall-discontinuity test.

name: Critic Overoptimization Curves (COC): measuring how far each cheap evaluator can be optimized before it stops tracking executed gains
one_line: From one small, stratified, prediction-powered executed sample, estimate for every cheap evaluator (Opus rubric, pairwise tournament, trained predictor, time-split matching, novelty distance) the realized gain it delivers as selection and optimization pressure rise. This tells OptiLex which signals it may hill-climb, and for how many steps.
closest_prior_work: Gao, Schulman & Hilton, 'Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization' (arXiv 2210.10760): RLHF against a synthetic gold reward model, not executed science. Si et al. 2026 (arXiv 2601.14525): RL on true execution reward collapsed to 2 ideas (119/128), with no critic curves. Red Queen Gödel Machine (arXiv 2606.26294): evaluators refreshed against ground-truth anchor sets. SciStyleBench (arXiv 2608.01666): style perturbations of fixed-substance ideas, open-model judges only. Wen/Mule outcome predictors: accuracy on fixed test pools. AlphaResearch RM (arXiv 2511.08522): 28.5% false rejections. HindSight (arXiv 2603.15164): false zeros acknowledged but never measured. Prediction-powered inference for LLM-judge evaluation: e.g. arXiv 2606.05308, and the GLIDE library (arXiv 2605.31278). An arXiv API search found no PPI application to executed research-idea outcomes.
why_novel: Every existing test of idea critics reports accuracy on a fixed pool (AUC, pairwise accuracy, kappa). That is the wrong quantity for a component the engine will select and optimize against. COC is the first to measure, with executed ground truth, how the realized value of research-idea critics behaves under rising selection pressure and under optimization pressure, separating presentation gameability (patch-locked rewrites) from substance overoptimization. The design choice that makes this affordable is prediction-powered, stratified execution: one small executed sample yields valid selection curves for all evaluators at once. It also produces the first measured false-zero rate for time-split matching metrics (an open gap in the map), and turns the output into an operational rule for the engine: which signal may be optimized, and for at most how many steps.
evidence_basis:
Critics fail under pressure in ways fixed-pool accuracy hides:
- CycleResearcher scored 5.36 vs 5.24 for human preprints while its results were fabricated.
- Jr. AI Scientist's higher-scoring papers had more hallucinated numbers.
- Laundering rewrites raise AI review scores +0.45.
- Style changes top-30 membership by 15.9%, and direct-judge substance recognition is 0.504.
- Pairwise preferences flip 35% vs 9% for absolute scores under distractors.
- Judge selective accuracy falls from 82.8% to 56.9% after >=3 accumulated successes (Rehearse).
- SoundnessBench: Opus 4.6 passes 71.8% of low-soundness proposals.

Cheap signals can anti-predict:
- HindSight: rho = -0.29 with judged novelty.
- MLRC-Bench: innovativeness vs effectiveness -0.06.
- Our pilot judge: 53% self-agreement.

Optimizing even a true reward collapses diversity (Si et al.). Selection on evaluation noise drove the >10% validation-to-test drops in Gideoni et al.

Small trained predictors beat frontier judges (77.1% vs GPT-5's 61.1%) but have never been tested under optimization pressure. The map lists 'the Goodhart curve for idea critics' and 'the false-zero rate of time-split metrics' as unmeasured.

Verified this session: 2210.10760, 2301.09633, 2603.15164, and the PPI-for-LLM-eval literature (arXiv API). Other numbers come from the checked map.
first_experiment:
Scoring:
- Generate 600 ideas across 4 generators (≈$26 at the measured $0.044 per idea).
- Score all with E1 ×2 (≈$12), E2 with about 3,000 swapped comparisons (≈$30), E6 and E7 (≈$0, embeddings).

Execution:
- Stratified sample of 60 ideas with known inclusion probabilities.
- 120 implementations (≈$150) and 720 proxy runs (≈$60-180).
- Patch-locked rewrite test on 30 executed ideas × 4 rounds against E1 and E2 (≈$15, no execution).

Total ≈$290-410. Substance-Goodhart rounds are deferred to phase 2.

Pre-registered, falsifiable predictions from the literature:
P1: E1 (Opus absolute rubric) is not hill-climbable. The 90% PPI CI of V_E1(1/8) includes 0. If instead V_E1(1/8) >= log(1.11) with CI > 0, the chance-level-judge finding does not transfer to Opus 5.5 on efficiency ideas, and E1 becomes a licensed filter.
P2: Time-split matching has a false-zero rate >= 30% among ideas beating 1.11x. If < 10%, E6 is declared a safe cheap proxy.
P3: Patch-locked rewrites raise E1 by >= 1.0 point on the 10-point scale and move >= 20% of ideas across the top-1/8 cutoff, which marks E1 as unsafe as an optimization target. The prediction for E2 on canonicalized cards is < 10%.

Method success criterion: PPI CIs are <= 60% of the width of executed-only CIs for at least one evaluator, which is equivalent to about a 2.8x saving in executions.
evaluation:
Ground truth is execution only: effective-data multiplier on hidden held-out loss, 2 independent implementations per idea, paired seeds, a frozen evaluator, and NVML energy. LLM judges are the objects being audited, never referees.

Time-split matching is audited against execution rather than trusted.

Curves come with valid finite-sample CIs (Horvitz-Thompson plus PPI), and each evaluator's license (hill-climbable yes/no, with k*) is set by pre-registered numeric thresholds.
cost_estimate: First round ≈$290-410. Phase 2 substance-Goodhart curves: ≈$150-250 per evaluator (about 12 ideas × 4 execution checkpoints × 2 implementations). Quarterly re-anchoring ≈$400-600. Once CHSP labels exist, E4 (the trained predictor) is nearly free to add, and its license is decided with the same data.
risks:
1) Power. With about 60 executed ideas and perhaps 10-20% positives, the curves at q <= 1/16 will be wide; PPI helps only as much as the cheap scores correlate with outcomes. Accumulate across rounds.
2) Stratifying on the evaluators themselves can reduce coverage of regions they all score low. Keep a uniform-random stratum of >= 20% of executions.
3) Pool composition sets the curves: an evaluator licensed on today's generators may fail on tomorrow's. Hence the quarterly re-anchoring, and licenses tied to a generator version.
4) The diff-locked rewrite test captures presentation gaming only. Substance gaming needs the costlier phase-2 curves.
5) Proxy-scale ground truth may itself mis-rank ideas relative to scale (about 20% of pairwise calls in DataDecide), so licenses apply at proxy scale.
6) Prior-art search used arXiv API queries only (web search budget exhausted).
